det_01.label: Where the data comes from: Wikidata SPARQL
det_01.content: Every row in this dataset was pulled from Wikidata's free SPARQL endpoint on 2026-05-24. A college is defined as any item that is an 'instance of' the class 'college of the University of Oxford' (Q2581649). Founding years are read from the 'inception' property (P571), founders from 'founded by' (P112), and namesakes from 'named after' (P138). Because Wikidata is a crowd-curated, CC0-licensed knowledge base, the dataset is fully reproducible by anyone with the query — but it also inherits Wikidata's editorial choices. It deliberately mixes the ~39 living colleges with long-dead ones, and a few entries (Examination Schools, Greek College) are really administrative or scholarly bodies rather than residential colleges. The data should be read as a snapshot of how Wikidata models Oxford, not as an official register.

sources.title: Wikidata
facts: Colleges identified as instance of college of the University of Oxford (Q2581649)
Inception P571 gives founding year, founded-by P112 gives founder, named-after P138 gives namesake
Wikidata is CC0-licensed and queryable for free via SPARQL

det_02.label: Three colleges, one unsolvable argument about age
det_02.content: Oxford's oldest-college title has three claimants and no referee, because each rests on a different definition of 'oldest'. University College (1249) points to the earliest money: a bequest in the 1249 will of William of Durham to support Oxford scholars. Balliol (c.1263) claims the longest unbroken physical presence — a house of scholars living on its founder's land on the present Broad Street site, continuously ever since. Merton (1264) holds the oldest formal constitution: Walter de Merton gave it statutes that made it a self-governing college, something Balliol and Univ lacked until the 1280s. All three dates fall inside a fifteen-year window, the medieval records are thin and disputed, and members of each college still cheerfully reject the others' claims. There is, in effect, no correct answer — which is exactly what makes it a good story.

sources.title: Q&A: oldest established — Balliol College Archives
facts: Balliol founded c.1263 as a house of scholars on land owned by its founder, on its present Broad Street site, continuously since
University College traces its claim to William of Durham's 1249 bequest

sources.title: Balliol College — Wikipedia
facts: The three oldest colleges (University, Balliol, Merton) were established between 1249 and 1264
There is dispute over the exact order and when each began taking students

det_03.label: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth
det_03.content: The 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations — but much of that count is churn, not pure expansion. Henry VIII's Reformation dissolved Oxford's monastic colleges: Gloucester College fell in 1539, St Mary's College in 1540, as the suppression of the monasteries cut off the religious orders that staffed them. At the same moment, new colleges rose from the rubble, often on the same stone. Cardinal Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell from favour, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — which doubles as the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. So the 16th-century 'boom' is partly a single institution being killed and reborn under three names, all of which survive as separate rows in the data.

facts: Cardinal College was suppressed after Wolsey's fall and refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532
Refounded as Christ Church in 1546, also serving as the cathedral of the Diocese of Oxford

det_04.label: 1878–1893: the women's colleges arrive
det_04.content: The 19th-century cluster in the data is not just more colleges — it is a change in who Oxford was for. Lady Margaret Hall (1878) was the first women's college; Somerville opened in 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination. St Anne's (1879), St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed within fifteen years. The catch: these colleges existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees. Women attended lectures and sat examinations but were not full members of the University until 1920. So a row dated 1878 marks the founding of an institution whose students could not graduate for another forty-two years — the dataset records the building before it records the right.

facts: Lady Margaret Hall founded 1878 as the first women's college; first students 1879
Somerville Hall opened 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination

The first women had degrees conferred in October 1920

det_05.label: The modern wave: philanthropists, mergers, and Reuben (2019)
det_05.content: The 20th–21st century foundations are dominated by graduate colleges endowed by industrial and financial wealth: Nuffield (1937, the motor magnate Lord Nuffield), Wolfson (1965, Isaac Wolfson), Kellogg (1990, the cereal fortune) and Reuben (2019). Reuben is the newest college in the dataset and the first new college at Oxford since Kellogg in 1990. It was approved by Congregation in May 2019 as 'Parks College', then renamed after an £80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation in 2020, and took its first graduate students in 2021 in the former Radcliffe Science Library. Green Templeton (2008) is a different kind of entry: it is a merger of Green College and Templeton College (1965), which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear as separate rows — the data captures a marriage and both of its partners.

det_06.label: Coats of arms and namesakes as a social history
det_06.content: Read the founder and namesake columns top to bottom and you get a compact social history of who held wealth and power in England across eight centuries. The medieval founders are bishops and royal clerks — Walter de Merton, William of Wykeham, William Waynflete. The Tudor era brings monarchs and prelates — Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, Cardinal Wolsey, Bishop Foxe. The modern era brings industrialists and financiers — Lord Nuffield, Isaac Wolfson, the Reuben brothers. The namesakes split the same way: early colleges are named for saints and feast days (Mary Magdalene, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity), while later ones are named for the benefactor's own surname. The colleges' heraldic coats of arms encode this lineage visually — each crest borrows the arms of its founder or patron — which is why the real crests are the natural visual spine for this story.

sources.title: Colleges of the University of Oxford — Wikipedia
facts: Colleges were founded by a mix of clergy, royalty and modern philanthropists
College coats of arms frequently derive from the arms of the founder or namesake

det_07.label: Caveats the analyst must respect
det_07.content: Several traps lurk in the data. (1) It blends current colleges with defunct, dissolved and merged ones — Rewley Abbey, Gloucester, Durham, Canterbury, Cardinal, King Henry VIII's, St Mary's, St Bernard's, Greek College, Templeton, Examination Schools — so any 'typical Oxford college' statistic must separate the ~39 survivors from the full historical set. (2) Two rows (Harris Manchester, St Bernard's) have a blank founding year and must be dropped from year-based math. (3) Medieval dates are approximate and disputed; 1249/1263/1264 are nominal. (4) Founder and namesake fields are often blank and sometimes hold multiple semicolon-separated names (Balliol, Christ Church, Green Templeton) that must be split before counting people. (5) The century table includes an 'unknown' bucket of 2 — the two blank-year colleges.

sources.title: Wikidata
facts: Founder field can hold multiple semicolon-separated values
Some colleges have no inception date recorded

det_08.label: Rewley Abbey: the 1201 outlier that is not really a college
det_08.content: The single oldest row in the dataset, Rewley Abbey (1201), is also the one that should not be counted as a college at all in the modern sense. It was a Cistercian monastic studium — a house where monks studied — founded on the edge of Oxford and dissolved at the Reformation. It appears because Wikidata's class definition is generous, and it sits 48 years before University College's 1249 claim. Including it would let someone say 'Oxford's oldest college dates to 1201', which is technically in the data but historically misleading. It is the clearest example of why the dataset's caveats matter: the earliest number is not the earliest college.

sources.title: Rewley Abbey — Wikipedia
facts: Rewley Abbey was a Cistercian monastic house with a studium near Oxford
It was dissolved during the Reformation and is not a surviving college
